title: Compound probability and expected value
lede: And, or, at least one, and what you can expect to win or lose on average. The math casinos, insurers and professional traders live by.

sections.md:
## AND: multiply (for independent events)
Two events are **independent** if one happening doesn't change the odds of the other: separate coin flips, separate dice, separate trades.

**P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)**

P(two heads in a row) = 1/2 × 1/2 = **1/4**. P(three in a row) = 1/8. Each extra "and" makes the outcome **less** likely, fast.

sections.title: Losing streaks
sections.problem: Your system loses 60% of trades. What's the chance of 5 losses in a row?
steps: Each trade is independent, so multiply: 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.6⁵.
sections.answer: **About 7.8%**, roughly 1 in 13 stretches of five trades. Over a few hundred trades, a 5-loss streak is almost guaranteed. That's why your plan stops you at 2 losses a day and sizes so you can survive streaks.

sections.md:
## Dependent events: when the first changes the second
Draw two cards **without putting the first back**. Now the second draw depends on the first.

P(two aces) = P(ace first) × P(ace second, given an ace was taken)
= 4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2,652 = **1/221** ≈ 0.45%

With replacement it would be 4/52 × 4/52 = 1/169. Small difference here, huge difference in small groups.

## OR: add, then subtract the overlap
**P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)**

Why subtract? Anything that is **both** A and B got counted twice.

P(drawing a heart **or** a king) = 13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52 = **16/52 = 4/13**. The king of hearts was in both groups.

If A and B **can't both happen** (rolling a 2 or a 5 on one die), the overlap is 0, and you just add.

sections.q: P(rolling a 1 or a 6 on one die)?
sections.why: They can't both happen, so just add: 1/6 + 1/6 = **1/3**.

sections.md:
## At least one: use the complement
"At least one" problems are a trap if you try to count every way it can happen. Flip it:

**P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)**

This is the problem that **started probability theory**. In 1654 a gambler, the Chevalier de Méré, asked Blaise Pascal why betting on at least one 6 in 4 rolls of a die won money, but betting on at least one double-6 in 24 rolls of two dice lost. Pascal worked it out in letters with Pierre de Fermat.

sections.title: De Méré's first bet
sections.answer: **About 51.8%**: a small edge for the bettor. The double-6 bet comes out to about 49.1%, a small edge **against**. Tiny edges, repeated, decide who wins.

sections.md:
## Tree diagrams
For multi-step problems, draw a **tree**: each branch is an outcome with its probability. **Multiply along a path** to get that path's probability; **add across paths** that give the result you want. Every set of branches from one point must add to 1. When problems get confusing, the tree keeps you honest.

## Expected value: the average result per try
**Expected value (EV) = Σ (probability × payoff)** over every outcome. It's what you'd average per try over the long run.

**American roulette**, $1 on a single number: 38 pockets, pays 35 to 1.

EV = (1/38)(+35) + (37/38)(−1) = (35 − 37) ÷ 38 = **−$0.053**

You lose about 5.3 cents per dollar, on average, forever. Casinos don't need luck. They need EV and volume.

## Expected value in trading
Your plan's math is an expected-value calculation. Measured in **R** (your risk per trade):

**EV per trade = (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss)**

| Win rate | Avg win | Avg loss | EV per trade |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50% | 1R | 1R | 0 |
| 40% | 2R | 1R | 0.8 − 0.6 = **+0.2R** |
| 25% | 10R | 1R | 2.5 − 0.75 = **+1.75R** |
| 60% | 0.5R | 1R | 0.3 − 0.4 = **−0.1R** |

The last row is the trap: a 60% win rate that **loses money**. Win rate alone means nothing. Only EV matters.

At +1.75R per trade, risking $200, the long-run average is about **+$350 per trade**. But that average is built from a lot of −$200 days and a few huge ones. EV tells you the destination, not how smooth the road is.

sections.q: A system wins 70% of the time. Average win +$100, average loss −$300. EV per trade?
sections.why: 0.7 × 100 − 0.3 × 300 = 70 − 90 = **−$20**. A high win rate, losing money.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Multiplying non-independent events as if they were independent.** Two trades in the same direction on the same news aren't independent.
- **Forgetting to subtract the overlap** in OR problems.
- **Treating EV as a promise.** Positive EV wins over many trials. Over 10 trades, anything can happen. Size so you survive long enough for the average to show up.

practice.why: The first draw changes what's left for the second.

practice.q: System: 40% wins at +2R, 60% losses at −1R. EV per trade in R?
A bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. Draw 2 without replacement. P(both red), as a fraction's decimal to 3 places?
Your system wins 25% of trades. P(8 losses in a row)? Round to 3 decimals.
practice.why: P(loss) = 0.75. 0.75⁸ ≈ **0.100**, about 1 in 10. Over hundreds of trades, 8-loss streaks will happen several times. At $250 risk that's −$2,000, the whole Lucid max loss, unless your daily and weekly stops cut it off first.

practice.q: De Méré's second bet: P(at least one double-6 in 24 rolls of two dice)? Round to 3 decimals.
practice.why: P(no double-6 per roll) = 35/36. P(none in 24) = (35/36)²⁴ ≈ 0.509. P(at least one) = 1 − 0.509 ≈ **0.491**: a losing bet.
practice.hint: Use 1 − P(none). P(no double-6 on one roll) = 35/36.

practice.q: A system wins 30% of trades at an average +4R and loses 70% at −1R. Risking $200 per trade, what's the EV per trade in **dollars**?
practice.hint: Find EV in R first, then multiply by the dollar value of 1R.

practice.q: An insurance policy costs $500 a year. It pays $50,000 if your truck is totaled, which has a 0.5% chance per year. From the buyer's side, the EV is…
options: −$250: you pay for peace of mind
practice.why: EV = 0.005 × 50,000 − 500 = 250 − 500 = **−$250**. Insurance is negative EV for buyers on purpose; you pay to avoid a loss you couldn't survive. EV isn't the only thing that matters when one outcome would ruin you.
practice.hint: Expected payout = probability × payout. Then subtract the cost.
